The current loop treats the presence of a text block as a final answer and returns it to the user. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Return the text block to the user because text means the model is finished
Execute only the first tool call and ignore the second
Discard the text block and re-ask the question without tools
Rely on `stop_reason` (`tool_use`): execute both tool calls and send both `tool_result` blocks back together in one user message, then call the model again
Send each `tool_result` in a separate user message

questions.explanation: A response can mix text and multiple tool calls. `stop_reason: tool_use` means to execute every requested tool and return all results in one user message before continuing.

distractor_notes.A: The text is a preamble to tool calls; `stop_reason` says the model is waiting for results.
distractor_notes.B: The model requested both, and skipping one leaves an unanswered `tool_use`, which the API rejects.
distractor_notes.C: It loses the model's plan and abandons the tool workflow.
distractor_notes.E: The results for one assistant turn belong together in a single user message.

questions.stem: A refactor will take four sessions over two weeks. At the start of each session Claude has no memory of the previous ones and repeats earlier analysis and sometimes reverses decisions. Which practice best preserves continuity?

options.text: Rely on the model to remember; start each session with "continue the refactor"

Keep a progress notes file in the repo (decisions, completed steps, next steps, open questions), update it at the end of each session, and start the next session by referencing it (for example `@PROGRESS.md`)
Use one very long session and never clear it
Copy the entire previous transcript into the first message of each session
Put every intermediate finding into CLAUDE.md permanently

questions.explanation: Durable, curated state belongs in a file that any session can read: concise decisions and next steps, referenced explicitly at the start. That is cheaper and more reliable than replaying history.

distractor_notes.A: A new session has no access to the earlier conversation.
distractor_notes.C: Long sessions hit limits and compaction, which is the original problem.
distractor_notes.D: It consumes a large share of the window and buries the decisions in noise.
distractor_notes.E: It bloats always-loaded memory with transient, task-specific state.

questions.stem: Four tasks arrive. Which one is best executed directly, without plan mode?

options.text: Redesign the caching layer used by six services, with unknown consistency requirements
Fix a single-function off-by-one bug that a failing unit test already reproduces, in a well-understood module, on a feature branch
Split a monolith into services, choosing the boundaries yourself
Replace the ORM across the codebase
Introduce a new authorisation model requiring sign-off from the security team

questions.explanation: Direct execution suits small, well-scoped, easily reversible work with a clear success check. Plan mode is for large scope, uncertainty, difficult reversal or required review.

distractor_notes.A: Broad, uncertain and hard to reverse: explore and plan first.
distractor_notes.C: Architectural uncertainty is high; the approach must be planned and reviewed.
distractor_notes.D: Large scope and an irreversible-feeling change that needs review before implementation.
distractor_notes.E: Stakeholder approval is needed before implementation, which plan mode supports.

questions.stem: A pipeline's model reports 0.95 confidence on most fields and reviewers only check low-confidence ones. A labelled audit shows overall accuracy is 97%, but for handwritten forms it is 82% even at 0.95 confidence. Which change to the routing strategy is best?

options.text: Keep a single global threshold because overall accuracy is high
Review a random 1% of everything and stop tracking segments
Measure accuracy per segment (document type and field) on a labelled sample, and set separate thresholds or mandatory review for weaker segments such as handwritten forms
Lower the global threshold to 0.5 so fewer documents are reviewed
Trust the model's confidence and stop the labelled audits

questions.explanation: Confidence scores are useful only if calibrated against labelled data. Segmenting by document characteristics and fields reveals where thresholds should differ, and where human review is worth its cost.

distractor_notes.A: The aggregate hides a segment where errors are frequent.
distractor_notes.B: Random sampling dilutes review across mostly accurate segments.
distractor_notes.D: It reduces review of exactly the risky documents.
distractor_notes.E: The audit is what revealed that confidence is miscalibrated for some segments.

questions.stem: A project's `.mcp.json` defines a `github` server whose `env` uses `"GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"`. A developer starts Claude Code and the GitHub tools are missing. The token variable was exported in a different terminal window from the one that launched Claude Code. What is the right diagnosis and check?

options.text: The server needs `--scope user` to load any tools
MCP servers cannot use environment variable expansion; hard-code the token

The variable was not set in the environment that launched Claude Code, so the server failed to start; export it in that shell, restart, and confirm with `/mcp` that the server is connected and its tools are listed
Claude Code hides tools until the model asks for them by name
Delete `.mcp.json` and let Claude Code regenerate it

questions.explanation: Environment expansion reads the variable from the environment of the process that starts the server. When tools are missing, check that the variable is visible to that process and verify discovery with `/mcp`.

distractor_notes.A: Scope controls who sees the server, not whether its environment variables resolve.
distractor_notes.B: Expansion is supported and hard-coding a secret is the mistake to avoid.
distractor_notes.D: Discovered tools are listed; missing tools indicate a connection problem.
distractor_notes.E: Regeneration will not supply an unset variable.

questions.stem: A `get_sales(date)` tool has the description "Get sales." Users say "sales for last Tuesday", and the model passes the string "last Tuesday", which the backend rejects. Which improvement is most effective?

options.text: Specify the input format and an example in the parameter description (`YYYY-MM-DD`, e.g. 2026-03-04), state that relative dates must be resolved to an absolute date before calling, and constrain the parameter with a pattern
Rename the tool to `get_sales_data`
Change the parameter to accept any string and log failures
Make the backend accept natural-language dates by guessing what "last Tuesday" means
Add "be careful with dates" to the system prompt

questions.explanation: Input format specifications and examples in the description, with a schema constraint, tell the model exactly how to form arguments and prevent avoidable validation failures.

distractor_notes.B: A longer name says nothing about the input format.
distractor_notes.C: It removes validation and turns failures into silent errors.
distractor_notes.D: It hides ambiguity server-side, and the correct reference date is known to the caller, not the tool.
distractor_notes.E: It gives no concrete format to follow.

questions.stem: An agent is connected to two MCP servers that each expose a tool called `search`: one searches internal wiki pages, the other searches customer support tickets. The agent picks the wrong one about a third of the time. What is the best remedy?

options.text: Keep both named `search` and add "choose correctly" to the system prompt
Disable one server and use only the other
Give the tools distinct, descriptive names (for example `search_wiki_pages` and `search_support_tickets`) and descriptions that state what each covers, when to use it, and when not to
Swap the order the servers are listed so the right one comes first
Have both tools run on every request and merge the results

questions.explanation: Selection reliability comes from distinctive names and descriptions that spell out scope, when to use the tool and when not to, especially for tools with overlapping purposes.

distractor_notes.A: Identical names and vague guidance leave nothing to discriminate on.
distractor_notes.B: It removes a needed capability.
distractor_notes.D: Order is not a reliable selection signal.
distractor_notes.E: It doubles cost and mixes unrelated sources instead of selecting the right one.
